idiom_name: one generic builder class whose type parameter records the filled steps; build(this: Builder<Required>)
implementation_notes: TypeScript collapses the per-step interface chain into a single generic class: the type parameter accumulates the names of the steps already performed (Builder<Set extends string = never>) and build() is constrained with a this parameter - build(this: Builder<'url' | 'method'>) - so an incomplete chain has no build method to call. Conditional and template-literal types can even synthesize the setters from the target type (type Builder<T> = { [K in keyof T as `with${Capitalize<K & string>}`]: (v: T[K]) => Builder<Set | K> }), which removes the hand-written interfaces entirely while keeping the check static. This form enforces presence, not order: keep a separate stage type per step when the sequence itself must be pinned, since the generic builder accepts the required setters in any order.
pitfalls: The `as` casts that keep the fluent generic compiling are unchecked: a setter that forgets to add its own key to the type parameter leaves build() callable too early, and nothing at run time notices.
Type-only enforcement disappears at run time and across any/`as unknown` boundaries - a caller can cast a half-built object to Req; keep runtime validation for data that crosses a boundary.

Synthesized setter types (template-literal keys, Required/Optional key helpers) treat `?` fields inconsistently unless the helpers are chosen deliberately; pin the semantics and test the negative case with @ts-expect-error.
